foundations.title: Practice: Foundations
foundations.intro: Use these questions after the Foundations section. They cover the alphabets, pronunciation, the case endings, the Greek article and the verb “to be”. Answers are in the answer key.

qs.text: Match each Greek letter with its name.
Match each Greek letter with its sound (the Erasmian pronunciation used in most classrooms).
right: ch as in Scottish loch or German Bach

qs.text: Write these Greek words in Roman letters: (a) λόγος (b) θεός (c) ψυχή (d) Χριστός (e) ἁμαρτία (f) ἄγγελος
In ἄγγελος (angel), the letters γγ are pronounced:
The mark ‘ over the first letter of ἁμαρτία (sin) is:
opts: a smooth breathing, which has no sound
a rough breathing, which adds an h-sound

qs.text: In τῷ λόγῳ the little ι written under each ω is an iota subscript. Which case does it often mark?
On which syllables can a Greek accent stand?
opts: only on one of the last three syllables

qs.text: False friends: these Greek capitals look like Latin letters but stand for other sounds. Match each with its sound.
In the restored classical pronunciation of Latin, how is the c of caelum (heaven) said?
opts: k, as in cat: c is always hard

qs.text: In classical Latin, the letter v (as in vīnum, wine) is said like English:
Give the case and number of each form of λόγος (word): (a) λόγον (b) λόγου (c) λόγοις (d) λόγοι (e) λόγων (f) λόγῳ
Give the case and number of each form of ἀρχή (beginning): (a) ἀρχῆς (b) ἀρχήν (c) ἀρχαῖς (d) ἀρχάς
Give every possible case and number for these Latin forms: (a) dominum (b) dominōrum (c) dominīs (d) puellam (e) puellae
ἔργα (works) and verba (words) are both plural. Which statement explains their endings?
opts: Neuter plurals end in -α (Greek) and -a (Latin) in the nominative and accusative

qs.text: Match each form of the Greek article with its description.
Supply the right form of the article (it must agree in case, number and gender): (a) ___ λόγοι (b) ___ ἔργα (nominative) (c) ___ καρδίᾳ (d) ___ ἀνθρώπων
Match each present-tense form of εἰμί (I am) with the Latin form of sum that means the same.
Translate, and give the person and number: (a) ἐσμέν (b) εἰσίν (c) estis (d) sum
In John 1:1, Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος / In principiō erat Verbum, the verbs ἦν and erat are:
Greek λύομεν, λύετε, λύουσι(ν) (we, you all, they loose) match Latin amāmus, amātis, amant (we, you all, they love). Which Latin ending matches each Greek ending -μεν, -τε, -ουσι(ν)?
In Ἐν ἀρχῇ (Greek) and In principiō (Latin), what case follows each preposition?
opts: dative in Greek, ablative in Latin

qs.text: Which case does Latin have that Greek does not?
ὁ κύων δάκνει τὸν ἄνθρωπον and τὸν ἄνθρωπον δάκνει ὁ κύων: who bites whom in each sentence, and how can you tell?
Latin has no word for “the” or “a”. Give two ways to translate verbum bonum, then translate verbum bonum est.
Match each Greek pronoun with the Latin pronoun that does the same job.
λόγος and verbum both mean “word”. What about their gender?
opts: λόγος is masculine, verbum is neuter
λόγος is neuter, verbum is masculine

matthew.title: Practice: Matthew
matthew.intro: These questions use the seven passages from Matthew: the core words they introduce, forms to parse, places where the Latin differs from the Greek, and three verses to read at sight.

qs.text: Match each Greek word with its meaning.
Match each Greek verb with its meaning.
Match each Latin word with its meaning.
Match each Greek word with the Latin word Jerome used for it.
Which three Greek words from Matthew never stand first in their clause?
Greek has two words for “not”. In ὁ μὴ ὢν μετ’ ἐμοῦ (Matthew 12:30), why is it μή and not οὐ?
opts: μή is used before a vowel
μή is the negative used with participles
μή is the Latin form of οὐ

qs.text: “Not” is spelled οὐ, οὐκ or οὐχ. Which spelling stands before (a) ἀδικῶ (b) ὡς (c) λέγω? Give the rule.
οὐχὶ δηναρίου συνεφώνησάς μοι; (Matthew 20:13) begins with οὐχί. What answer does the question expect, and which Latin word does the same job?
Parse ἀκούσατε (Matthew 13:18): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse δεχόμενος (Matthew 10:40): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse ἐκβάλετε (Matthew 22:13): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse εἶπεν (Matthew 20:13): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse ἔσται (Matthew 22:13): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse χεῖρας (Matthew 22:13): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse οὐρανῶν (Matthew 23:13): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse ὑμῖν (Matthew 23:13): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse εἰσελθεῖν (Matthew 23:13): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse ἀποστείλαντα (Matthew 10:40): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse the Latin audīte (Matthew 13:18): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse the Latin hominēs (Matthew 23:13): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Matthew 10:40: Greek says ὁ δεχόμενος ὑμᾶς, “the (one) welcoming you”. Latin says quī recipit vōs, “who receives you”. Why the change?
Matthew 22:13: Greek δήσαντες … πόδας καὶ χεῖρας means “having tied (his) feet and hands”. Latin has ligātīs manibus et pedibus ejus, “his hands and feet having been tied”. Why?
Matthew 5:7: Greek ἐλεηθήσονται means “they will be shown mercy”. Latin has two words, misericordiam cōnsequentur. Why?
Matthew 20:13: Greek οὐκ ἀδικῶ σε has σε in the accusative. Latin nōn faciō tibi injūriam has tibi in the dative. Why?
Matthew 23:13: Greek ἔμπροσθεν τῶν ἀνθρώπων has a genitive; Latin ante hominēs has an accusative. Why do the cases differ?
Sight reading (Matthew 7:1, not one of the video passages). Translate the Greek and the Latin.
extra: Greek: Μὴ κρίνετε, ἵνα μὴ κριθῆτε·
Latin: Nolite judicare, ut non judicemini.
Help: κρίνω = to judge; κριθῆτε is its aorist passive subjunctive; ἵνα = so that; nōlīte + infinitive = do not …; jūdicō = to judge.

qs.text: Sight reading (Matthew 25:12, not one of the video passages). Translate the Greek and the Latin.
extra: Greek: ὁ δὲ ἀποκριθεὶς εἶπεν· Ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, οὐκ οἶδα ὑμᾶς.
Latin: At ille respondens, ait: Amen dico vobis, nescio vos.
Help: ἀμήν / āmēn = amen, truly; οἶδα = I know; nesciō = I do not know; ait = he says, he said.

qs.text: Sight reading (Matthew 16:15, not one of the video passages). Translate the Greek and the Latin.
extra: Greek: λέγει αὐτοῖς· Ὑμεῖς δὲ τίνα με λέγετε εἶναι;
Latin: Dicit illis Jesus: Vos autem, quem me esse dicitis?
Help: τίνα = whom? (accusative of τίς); εἶναι / esse = to be; quem = whom?

Mark’s favorite word εὐθύς means:

qs.text: In Mark 13:10, τὰ ἔθνη (plural of ἔθνος) refers to:

qs.text: Mark 1:22, ἦν … διδάσκων αὐτούς, is best translated:
Parse ἦλθον (Mark 1:29): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse ἔρχονται (Mark 2:3): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse οἴδατε (Mark 4:13): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse γνώσεσθε (Mark 4:13): give its dictionary form and a full parse.

Parse the Latin vēnērunt (Mark 1:29): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse the Latin dedit (Mark 14:23): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Mark 6:47: Greek ὀψίας γενομένης is a genitive absolute, “evening having come”. Latin says cum sērō esset, “when it was late”. What has the Latin done?
Mark 2:3: Greek αἰρόμενον ὑπὸ τεσσάρων means “being carried by four”. Latin has quī ā quatuor portābātur, “who was being carried by four”. Why a clause?
Mark 15:5: Greek ὥστε θαυμάζειν τὸν Πιλᾶτον has an infinitive with Pilate in the accusative. Latin has ita ut mīrārētur Pīlātus. Explain both.
Mark 5:30: Greek ἥψατο τῶν ἱματίων puts “the clothes” in the genitive. Latin tetigit vestīmenta uses the accusative. Why?
Mark 5:17: Greek παρακαλεῖν αὐτὸν ἀπελθεῖν, “to beg him to go away”, uses an infinitive. Latin says rogāre eum ut discēderet. Why?
Sight reading (Mark 4:3, not one of the video passages). Translate the Greek and the Latin.
extra: Greek: Ἀκούετε. ἰδοὺ ἐξῆλθεν ὁ σπείρων σπεῖραι.
Latin: Audite: ecce exiit seminans ad seminandum.
Help: σπείρω / sēminō = to sow; σπεῖραι is the aorist infinitive; ad sēminandum = for sowing (a gerund).

qs.text: Sight reading (Mark 15:13, not one of the video passages). Translate the Greek and the Latin.
extra: Greek: οἱ δὲ πάλιν ἔκραξαν· Σταύρωσον αὐτόν.
Latin: At illi iterum clamaverunt: Crucifige eum.
Help: κράζω = to cry out; clāmō = to shout.

qs.text: Sight reading (Mark 15:2, not one of the video passages). Translate the Greek and the Latin.
extra: Greek: καὶ ἐπηρώτησεν αὐτὸν ὁ Πιλᾶτος· Σὺ εἶ ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων; ὁ δὲ ἀποκριθεὶς αὐτῷ λέγει· Σὺ λέγεις.
Latin: Et interrogavit eum Pilatus: Tu es rex Judaeorum? At ille respondens, ait illi: Tu dicis.
Help: ἐπερωτάω = to ask, question; Ἰουδαῖος = Jew; Jūdaeus = Jew; ait = he says, he said.

Luke 2:8: ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ τῇ αὐτῇ. With the article, αὐτός means:

Luke 18:18: Greek τί ποιήσας … means “having done what …?”, with an aorist participle. Latin has quid faciēns, a present participle, “doing what?” Why?
Luke 14:20: Greek γυναῖκα ἔγημα, “I married a wife”. Latin uxōrem dūxī means word for word “I led a wife”. Why?
Luke 22:39: Greek ἠκολούθησαν δὲ αὐτῷ has “him” in the dative. Latin secūtī sunt autem illum has the accusative. Why?
Luke 1:38: Mary says γένοιτό μοι, an optative. Latin says fīat mihi, a subjunctive. Why?
Luke 1:53: πεινῶντας ἐνέπλησεν ἀγαθῶν, “he filled the hungry with good things”, uses the genitive ἀγαθῶν. Latin ēsurientēs implēvit bonīs uses the ablative. Why?
Sight reading (Luke 15:11, not one of the video passages). Translate the Greek and the Latin.
extra: Greek: Εἶπεν δέ· Ἄνθρωπός τις εἶχεν δύο υἱούς.
Latin: Ait autem: Homo quidam habuit duos filios:
Help: εἶχεν = he had (imperfect of ἔχω); δύο / duo = two (duōs is accusative); ait = he said.

qs.text: Sight reading (Luke 13:30, not one of the video passages). Translate the Greek and the Latin.
extra: Greek: καὶ ἰδοὺ εἰσὶν ἔσχατοι οἳ ἔσονται πρῶτοι, καὶ εἰσὶν πρῶτοι οἳ ἔσονται ἔσχατοι.
Latin: Et ecce sunt novissimi qui erunt primi, et sunt primi qui erunt novissimi.
Help: ἔσχατος = last; Latin novissimus (word for word “newest”) is used for “last”; οἵ = who (plural of ὅς).

qs.text: Sight reading (Luke 20:25, not one of the video passages). Translate the Greek and the Latin.
extra: Greek: ὁ δὲ εἶπεν πρὸς αὐτούς· Τοίνυν ἀπόδοτε τὰ Καίσαρος Καίσαρι καὶ τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ τῷ θεῷ.
Latin: Et ait illis: Reddite ergo quae sunt Caesaris, Caesari: et quae sunt Dei, Deo.
Help: τοίνυν = then, therefore; Καῖσαρ (genitive Καίσαρος, dative Καίσαρι) = Caesar; ἀπόδοτε = give back! (aorist imperative of ἀποδίδωμι); reddō = give back.

john.title: Practice: John
john.intro: These questions use the twenty-six passages from John: the core words they introduce, forms to parse, places where the Latin differs from the Greek, and three verses to read at sight.

qs.text: Match each Greek noun with its meaning.
Match each Greek verb with its meaning.
Match each Latin word with its meaning.
Match each Greek word with the Latin word used for it in John.
John 9:41: εἰ τυφλοὶ ἦτε, οὐκ ἂν εἴχετε ἁμαρτίαν. What does the little word ἄν do?
opts: it marks the result as unreal: “you would have”
it turns the sentence into a question

qs.text: John 13:34: ἵνα ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλήλους. ἀλλήλους means:
Which Greek word points to “that (one)”, farther off, like Latin ille?
Parse ἠθέλησεν (John 1:43): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse λύσατε (John 2:19): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse ἐγερῶ (John 2:19): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse προσκυνήσετε (John 4:21): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse φαγεῖν (John 4:33): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse ἀγαπᾶτε (John 13:34): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse ἠγάπησα (John 13:34): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse γέγραφα (John 19:22): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse ἡμέραις (John 2:19): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse the Latin vidēbit (John 8:51): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
John 1:2: Greek οὗτος ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ, “this one (masculine) was in the beginning”. Latin has hoc erat in prīncipiō, with the neuter hoc. Why?
John 1:43: Greek ἀκολούθει μοι, “follow me”, has μοι in the dative. Latin sequere mē has the accusative. Why?
John 10:21: Greek ταῦτα τὰ ῥήματα οὐκ ἔστιν … has a singular verb with a plural subject. Latin says haec verba nōn sunt … Why the difference?
John 8:51: Greek θάνατον οὐ μὴ θεωρήσῃ uses οὐ μή with an aorist subjunctive. Latin says mortem nōn vidēbit, with a future. Why?
John 9:41: εἰ τυφλοὶ ἦτε, οὐκ ἂν εἴχετε ἁμαρτίαν becomes sī caecī essētis, nōn habērētis peccātum. How does each language mark the condition as unreal?
Sight reading (John 1:10, not one of the video passages). Translate the Greek and the Latin.
extra: Greek: Ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ ἦν, καὶ ὁ κόσμος δι’ αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο, καὶ ὁ κόσμος αὐτὸν οὐκ ἔγνω.
Latin: In mundo erat, et mundus per ipsum factus est, et mundus eum non cognovit.
Help: δι’ = διά, through (with the genitive); ἐγένετο = came to be (aorist of γίνομαι); ἔγνω = knew (aorist of γινώσκω); factus est = came to be, was made; cognōvit = knew, recognized.

qs.text: Sight reading (John 10:30, not one of the video passages). Translate the Greek and the Latin.
extra: Greek: ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν.
Latin: Ego et Pater unum sumus.
Help: ἕν = one (neuter of εἷς); ūnum = one (neuter of ūnus).

qs.text: Sight reading (John 13:17, not one of the video passages). Translate the Greek and the Latin.
extra: Greek: εἰ ταῦτα οἴδατε, μακάριοί ἐστε ἐὰν ποιῆτε αὐτά.
Latin: Si haec scitis, beati eritis si feceritis ea.
Help: οἴδατε = you know (οἶδα); scītis = you know (sciō); ποιῆτε = you do (present subjunctive of ποιέω after ἐάν); fēceritis = you will have done.

acts.title: Practice: Acts
acts.intro: These questions use the three passages from Acts: the core words they introduce, forms to parse, places where the Latin differs from the Greek, and three more verses from Acts to read at sight.

qs.text: Match each Greek word with its meaning.
right: holy; plural as a noun: saints

qs.text: Match each Greek word with the Latin word used for it in Acts.
Acts 19:6: ἐλάλουν τε γλώσσαις. The little word τε means “and”. Where does it stand?
opts: never first: after the first word of what it joins
only at the end of a sentence

qs.text: Acts 13:24: πρὸ προσώπου τῆς εἰσόδου αὐτοῦ. The preposition πρό means:
Latin loquor (loquēbantur, Acts 19:6) is a deponent verb. This means it is:
opts: passive in form but active in meaning

qs.text: Parse διερχόμενον (Acts 9:32): give its dictionary form and a full parse.
Parse κατοικοῦντας (Acts 9:32): give its dictionary form and a full parse.

Acts 9:32: Greek ἐγένετο … Πέτρον … κατελθεῖν has Peter in the accusative with an infinitive (“it happened for Peter to come down”). Latin has factum est … ut Petrus … dēvenīret. Why is Petrus nominative?
Acts 13:24: Greek προκηρύξαντος Ἰωάννου (genitive) becomes Latin praedicante Jōanne (ablative). What construction is each?
Acts 19:5: Greek ἀκούσαντες, “having heard” (an active participle agreeing with the subject), becomes Latin hīs audītīs, “these things having been heard”. Why?
Acts 19:5: Greek εἰς τὸ ὄνομα, with the accusative, means “into the name”. Latin has in nōmine. What has changed?
Sight reading (Acts 9:9, not one of the video passages). Translate the Greek and the Latin.
extra: Greek: καὶ ἦν ἡμέρας τρεῖς μὴ βλέπων, καὶ οὐκ ἔφαγεν οὐδὲ ἔπιεν.
Latin: Et erat ibi tribus diebus non videns, et non manducavit, neque bibit.
Help: ἔφαγεν = he ate (aorist of ἐσθίω); ἔπιεν = he drank (aorist of πίνω); mandūcō = to eat; bibō = to drink; neque = and not, nor.

qs.text: Sight reading (Acts 4:20, not one of the video passages). Translate the Greek and the Latin.
extra: Greek: οὐ δυνάμεθα γὰρ ἡμεῖς ἃ εἴδαμεν καὶ ἠκούσαμεν μὴ λαλεῖν.
Latin: Non enim possumus quae vidimus et audivimus non loqui.
Help: δυνάμεθα = we are able (δύναμαι); ἅ / quae = the things which; εἴδαμεν = we saw (aorist of ὁράω); loquī = to speak (infinitive of loquor).

qs.text: Sight reading (Acts 26:15, not one of the video passages). Translate the Greek and the Latin.
extra: Greek: ἐγὼ δὲ εἶπα· Τίς εἶ, κύριε; ὁ δὲ κύριος εἶπεν· Ἐγώ εἰμι Ἰησοῦς ὃν σὺ διώκεις·
Latin: Ego autem dixi: Quis es, domine? Dominus autem dixit: Ego sum Jesus, quem tu persequeris.
Help: εἶπα = I said; διώκω = to pursue, persecute; persequor (deponent) = to persecute.

1.a: 1–d, 2–a, 3–f, 4–h, 5–g, 6–c, 7–b, 8–e (η = eta; θ = theta; λ = lambda; ξ = xi; ρ = rho; φ = phi; χ = chi; ψ = psi)

2.a: 1–b, 2–d, 3–h, 4–a, 5–f, 6–g, 7–c, 8–e (θ = th as in thin; φ = ph as in phone; χ = ch as in Scottish loch or German Bach; ψ = ps as in lips; ξ = x as in ax (ks); ζ = dz, as in zeal said “dzeal”; η = long e, as in they; ω = long o, as in tone)

3.a: (a) logos (b) theos (c) psychē (d) Christos (e) hamartia (f) angelos
3.why: θ = th, ψ = ps, η = ē, υ = y, χ = ch; the rough breathing on ἁ adds an h; γγ is written and said ng.

4.why: Gamma before another gamma (or before κ, ξ, χ) is said ng.

5.a: (b) a rough breathing, which adds an h-sound
5.why: Every word that begins with a vowel carries a breathing: rough ‘ = h, smooth ’ = no sound. So ἁμαρτία is hamartia.

6.why: The dative singular of the first and second declensions ends in -ῳ or -ῃ/-ᾳ: τῷ λόγῳ, τῇ ἀρχῇ.

7.a: (c) only on one of the last three syllables
7.why: The accent never goes further back than the third syllable from the end. Latin stress obeys the same three-syllable window.

8.a: 1–d, 2–c, 3–a, 4–b (Η = long e (ē); Ρ = r; Χ = ch; Υ = u / y (like French u))

9.a: (a) k, as in cat: c is always hard
9.why: Classical Latin c is always k. Church Latin softens c before e and i, so caelum becomes “chay-loom”.

10.why: Classical v is w: vīnum is “wee-num”. Church Latin says v.

11.a: (a) accusative singular (b) genitive singular (c) dative plural (d) nominative plural (also vocative plural) (e) genitive plural (f) dative singular
11.why: -ος nom., -ου gen., -ῳ dat., -ον acc. singular; -οι nom., -ων gen., -οις dat., -ους acc. plural.

12.a: (a) genitive singular (b) accusative singular (c) dative plural (d) accusative plural
12.why: First declension: -η, -ης, -ῃ, -ην in the singular; -αι, -ων, -αις, -ας in the plural.

13.a: (a) accusative singular (b) genitive plural (c) dative or ablative plural (d) accusative singular (e) genitive singular, dative singular, or nominative (also vocative) plural (f) accusative singular
13.why: Latin endings often have more than one possible meaning; the rest of the sentence decides which.

14.a: (b) Neuter plurals end in -α (Greek) and -a (Latin) in the nominative and accusative
14.why: The neuter rule: the nominative and accusative are always alike, and the plural ends in -α / -a.

15.a: 1–d, 2–h, 3–f, 4–c, 5–a, 6–g, 7–e, 8–b (τοῦ = genitive singular, masculine or neuter; τῇ = dative singular feminine; τόν = accusative singular masculine; τούς = accusative plural masculine; τά = nominative or accusative plural neuter; αἱ = nominative plural feminine; τῶν = genitive plural, all three genders; τῷ = dative singular, masculine or neuter)

16.a: (a) οἱ λόγοι (b) τὰ ἔργα (c) τῇ καρδίᾳ (d) τῶν ἀνθρώπων
16.why: λόγοι nominative plural masculine; ἔργα nominative plural neuter; καρδίᾳ dative singular feminine; ἀνθρώπων genitive plural masculine.

17.a: 1–b, 2–c, 3–d, 4–a, 5–f, 6–e (εἰμί = sum; εἶ = es; ἐστί(ν) = est; ἐσμέν = sumus; ἐστέ = estis; εἰσί(ν) = sunt)

18.a: (a) we are, 1st person plural (b) they are, 3rd person plural (c) you (plural) are, 2nd person plural (d) I am, 1st person singular

19.why: ἦν is the imperfect of εἰμί; erat is the imperfect of sum.

20.why: The endings come from the same ancestor language.

21.a: (a) dative in Greek, ablative in Latin
21.why: Greek has no ablative; its dative does this job. Latin “in” with the ablative means “in”, with the accusative “into”.

22.why: Latin has six cases; Greek has five and splits the ablative’s jobs between the genitive (“from”) and the dative (“by, with, in”).

23.a: In both sentences the dog bites the man.
23.why: ὁ κύων is nominative (the subject); τὸν ἄνθρωπον is accusative (the object). Endings, not word order, carry the meaning.

24.a: verbum bonum: “a good word” or “the good word”; verbum bonum est: “the word is good”.
24.why: Context decides between “a” and “the”. Greek would say ὁ ἀγαθὸς λόγος (the good word) or ὁ λόγος ἀγαθός (the word is good).

25.a: 1–b, 2–a, 3–e, 4–h, 5–c, 6–g, 7–d, 8–f (ἐγώ = ego; σύ = tū; ἡμεῖς = nōs; ὑμεῖς = vōs; αὐτός (“-self”) = ipse; οὗτος = hic; ἐκεῖνος = ille; τίς = quis)

26.a: (c) λόγος is masculine, verbum is neuter
26.why: Grammatical gender belongs to the word, not the thing, and the two languages can differ.

1.a: 1–d, 2–h, 3–f, 4–e, 5–a, 6–g, 7–b, 8–c (μακάριος = blessed, happy; βασιλεύς = king; βασιλεία = kingdom, reign; χείρ = hand; πούς = foot; οὐρανός = heaven, sky; ἄνθρωπος = human being, person; παραβολή = parable)

2.a: 1–c, 2–d, 3–a, 4–f, 5–b, 6–g, 7–h, 8–e (ἀκούω = to hear, listen; λέγω = to say, speak; ἀποστέλλω = to send out; ἐκβάλλω = to throw out, drive out; εἰσέρχομαι = to go in, enter; ἀφίημι = to let, permit; forgive; ἀποκρίνομαι = to answer; δέχομαι = to receive, welcome)

3.a: 1–f, 2–e, 3–d, 4–h, 5–a, 6–g, 7–b, 8–c (quoniam = because, since; autem = but, however; now; enim = for (giving a reason); ergō = therefore, so; tunc = then, at that time; ibi = there; ante = before, in front of; vae = woe!)

4.a: 1–f, 2–h, 3–d, 4–g, 5–b, 6–c, 7–e, 8–a (βασιλεύς = rēx; βασιλεία = rēgnum; οὐρανός = caelum; χείρ = manus; πούς = pēs; ἄνθρωπος = homō; ἀκούω = audiō; εἷς = ūnus)

5.why: δέ (but), γάρ (for) and οὖν (so) are “second-position” words. Latin autem and enim behave the same way.

6.a: (b) μή is the negative used with participles
6.why: οὐ negates statements of fact (οὐκ ἀδικῶ σε); μή goes with participles, commands, subjunctives and infinitives.

7.a: (a) οὐκ ἀδικῶ (b) οὐχ ὡς (c) οὐ λέγω
7.why: οὐ before a consonant; οὐκ before a vowel with smooth breathing; οὐχ before a rough breathing.

8.why: οὐχί (a strong οὐ) opens a question that expects “yes”; so does Latin nōnne.

9.a: ἀκούω, “to hear, listen”: aorist active imperative, 2nd person plural
9.why: -σατε: the aorist sign σα plus the 2nd-plural ending -τε; no augment, because imperatives never take one.

10.a: δέχομαι, “to receive, welcome”: present middle participle, nominative singular masculine (deponent: middle form, active meaning)
10.why: -όμενος is the present middle/passive participle ending; the meaning is active: “welcoming”.

11.a: ἐκβάλλω, “to throw out, drive out”: aorist active imperative, 2nd person plural
11.why: Second aorist: the present stem βαλλ- loses one λ (βαλ-) and takes -ετε. In context, “throw (him) out!”

12.a: λέγω, “to say, speak”: aorist active indicative, 3rd person singular
12.why: εἶπον, εἶπες, εἶπεν is the aorist of λέγω, built on a different stem.

13.a: εἰμί, “to be”: future middle indicative, 3rd person singular
13.why: The future of εἰμί has middle endings: ἔσομαι, ἔσῃ, ἔσται. Latin: erit.

14.why: -ας is the accusative plural of the third declension (χείρ, χειρός).

15.a: οὐρανός, “heaven, sky”: noun, genitive plural masculine
15.why: -ων is genitive plural in every declension: τῶν οὐρανῶν, “of the heavens”.

16.why: ὑμῖν is “to/for you (plural)”; compare ἡμῖν “to/for us”.

17.a: εἰσέρχομαι, “to go in, enter”: aorist active infinitive
17.why: The second-aorist stem ελθ- (from ἔρχομαι) with the infinitive ending -εῖν.

18.a: ἀποστέλλω, “to send out”: aorist active participle, accusative singular masculine
18.why: A liquid aorist: the stem στειλ- (present στελλ-) takes no σ, so -αντα stands where λύσαντα has -σαντα. With τόν it is the object of δέχεται: “the one who sent me”.

19.a: audiō, audīre, audīvī, audītum, “to hear”: present active imperative, 2nd person plural
19.why: The 4th-conjugation stem audī- plus the plural command ending -te. Greek used an aorist command, ἀκούσατε; Latin has no aorist.

20.a: homō, hominis, m., “human being, person”: accusative plural (after ante)
20.why: -ēs is nominative or accusative plural in the 3rd declension; ante takes the accusative, so here it is accusative.

21.a: Latin has no article, so it cannot turn a participle into a noun with “the”. It uses a relative clause instead: quī (who) with an ordinary verb, recipit.

22.a: Latin has no active past participle (no word for “having tied”; only deponent verbs have one). It uses the perfect passive participle ligātus in an ablative absolute: “with his hands and feet tied”.

23.a: Greek has a one-word future passive. Latin has no single verb for “be shown mercy”, so it uses the noun misericordia (mercy) with cōnsequor (obtain): “they will obtain mercy”.

24.a: Latin turns “I wrong you” into “I do injury to you”. Injūriam is now the object (accusative), so the person wronged goes in the dative: tibi, “to you”.

25.a: Each preposition decides the case of its noun. ἔμπροσθεν takes the genitive; Latin ante takes the accusative. Both mean “in front of people”.

26.a: Greek and Latin: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.”
26.why: Greek forbids with μή + a present imperative (κρίνετε); Latin with nōlīte (“be unwilling”) + infinitive. Both then use a purpose clause with a subjunctive: ἵνα μὴ κριθῆτε / ut nōn jūdicēminī.

27.a: Greek: “But he answered and said, ‘Amen, I tell you, I do not know you.’” (word for word: “But he, answering, said …”). Latin: “But he, answering, said, ‘Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.’”
27.why: ὁ δὲ ἀποκριθεὶς εἶπεν is the same pattern as Matthew 20:13 (ὁ δὲ ἀποκριθεὶς … εἶπεν). Latin nesciō packs “not know” into one verb.

28.a: Greek: “He says to them, ‘But you, who do you say that I am?’” (word for word: “whom do you say me to be?”). Latin: “Jesus says to them, ‘But you, who do you say that I am?’”
28.why: Latin adds the name Jesus. Both languages put the subject of the infinitive in the accusative: με εἶναι / mē esse, “me to be”, so the question word is accusative too: τίνα / quem.

1.a: 1–g, 2–f, 3–a, 4–b, 5–h, 6–d, 7–c, 8–e (ἔρχομαι = to come, go; γινώσκω = to know, come to know; λαμβάνω = to take, receive; δίδωμι = to give; ποιέω = to do, make; ὁράω = to see; πιστεύω = to believe, trust; ἐγείρω = to raise, wake)

2.a: 1–e, 2–f, 3–a, 4–g, 5–b, 6–c, 7–h, 8–d (ὄχλος = crowd; θάλασσα = sea, lake; πλοῖον = boat; ὄνομα = name; ψυχή = soul, life, self; θάνατος = death; φωνή = voice, sound, cry; ὀφθαλμός = eye)

3.a: 1–d, 2–g, 3–a, 4–f, 5–b, 6–e, 7–h, 8–c (statim = at once, immediately; iterum = again; ecce = look! see!; dōnec = until; omnis = all, every; quis = who?; magnus = great, large, loud; nihil = nothing)

4.a: 1–d, 2–g, 3–a, 4–c, 5–h, 6–b, 7–e, 8–f (ἔρχομαι = veniō; δίδωμι = dō; λαμβάνω = accipiō; πιστεύω = crēdō; κύριος = dominus; μαθητής = discipulus; γῆ = terra; ὄνομα = nōmen)

5.why: Latin varies its word for it: prōtinus (1:29), cōnfestim (5:29), statim (5:30, 8:10).

6.a: (b) a purpose, “so that”, with a subjunctive
6.why: ἵνα + subjunctive = “so that / in order that”. Latin uses ut + subjunctive: ut prōderet eum illīs.

7.a: (b) the nations, often meaning the Gentiles

8.why: The imperfect of εἰμί + a present participle describes an ongoing past action. Latin copies the pattern: erat docēns.

9.a: ἔρχομαι, “to come, go”: aorist active indicative, 3rd person plural (here “they went”; the same form can also mean “I came”)
9.why: ἦλθον is the second aorist of ἔρχομαι: stem ελθ-, augmented to ἠλθ-.

10.a: ἔρχομαι, “to come, go”: present middle indicative, 3rd person plural (deponent: middle form, active meaning)
10.why: -ονται is the 3rd plural middle/passive ending. Mark uses the vivid present for a past event; Latin has the perfect vēnērunt.

11.a: οἶδα, “to know”: perfect active indicative, 2nd person plural (perfect form, present meaning: “you know”)
11.why: οἶδα has perfect forms only (οἶδα, οἶδας, οἶδεν … οἴδατε) with present meaning; its past “I knew” is the pluperfect ᾔδειν (ᾔδει, John 6:6).

12.a: γινώσκω, “to know, come to know”: future middle indicative, 2nd person plural
12.why: γινώσκω has a middle future: γνώσομαι. -σεσθε = future σ + 2nd plural middle ending -εσθε.

13.a: δίδωμι, “to give”: aorist active indicative, 3rd person singular
13.why: δίδωμι forms its aorist with κ: ἔδωκα, ἔδωκας, ἔδωκεν. Latin dedit, from dō, shares the root.

14.a: λαμβάνω, “to take, receive”: aorist active participle, nominative singular masculine
14.why: -ών on the second-aorist stem λαβ- (from λαμβάνω): “having taken”.

15.a: κηρύσσω, “to proclaim, preach”: aorist passive infinitive
15.why: -θῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive ending: “to be proclaimed”. Latin: praedicārī.

16.a: ἄγω, “to lead, go”: present active subjunctive, 1st person plural
16.why: The long vowel ω (ἄγωμεν, not ἄγομεν) marks the subjunctive; in the 1st person plural it means “let us …”: “let us go”.

17.a: σταυρόω, “to crucify”: aorist active imperative, 2nd person singular
17.why: -σον is the aorist imperative ending for one person: “crucify!”

18.a: veniō, venīre, vēnī, ventum, “to come”: perfect active indicative, 3rd person plural
18.why: The perfect stem vēn- (long e) plus -ērunt. It renders the Greek aorist ἦλθον: Latin has no separate aorist.

19.a: dō, dare, dedī, datum, “to give”: perfect active indicative, 3rd person singular
19.why: The perfect of dō is reduplicated: dedī, dedistī, dedit. Greek ἔδωκεν is the aorist of the related verb δίδωμι.

20.a: Latin has turned the Greek participle phrase into a clause: cum with the subjunctive (esset), its usual way of saying “when …”.
20.why: Greek loves participles; Latin often prefers a clause. Here the Latin also says “late” (sērō) instead of “evening”.

21.a: Latin has no present passive participle (no single word for “being carried”), so it uses a relative clause with an imperfect passive verb, portābātur.

22.a: After ὥστε (“so that”, result) Greek uses an infinitive whose subject goes in the accusative (τὸν Πιλᾶτον). Latin expresses result with ut + subjunctive (mīrārētur), so Pīlātus is an ordinary nominative subject.

23.a: Greek ἅπτω in the middle voice (“to touch”) takes the genitive. Latin tangō takes a plain accusative object.

24.a: After verbs of asking, Latin normally uses ut + subjunctive (“that he should go away”) instead of an infinitive.

25.a: Greek: “Listen! Look, the sower went out to sow.” (word for word: “the one sowing went out to sow”). Latin: “Listen: look, a sower went out to sow” (word for word: “for sowing”).
25.why: Greek ὁ σπείρων, article + participle, is “the sower”; Latin sēmināns has no article. Greek expresses purpose with the infinitive σπεῖραι, Latin with ad + gerund, ad sēminandum. ἐξῆλθεν (aorist of ἐξέρχομαι) = exiit (perfect of exeō).

26.a: Greek and Latin: “And they shouted again, ‘Crucify him!’” (Latin at illī: “but they”).
26.why: οἱ δέ, the article with δέ, marks a change of speaker: “and they”. σταύρωσον and crucifīge are both commands to one person.

27.a: Greek: “And Pilate questioned him, ‘Are you the king of the Jews?’ And he answered him and says, ‘You say so.’” (word for word: “he, answering him, says, ‘You say.’”). Latin: “And Pilate questioned him: ‘Are you the king of the Jews?’ But he, answering, said to him: ‘You say so.’”
27.why: Σὺ εἶ = Tū es, “you are”. ὁ δὲ ἀποκριθεὶς … λέγει = at ille respondēns ait: the Greek participle is kept as a Latin present participle.

1.a: 1–f, 2–h, 3–g, 4–c, 5–b, 6–e, 7–a, 8–d (ἡμέρα = day; καρδία = heart; πατήρ = father; μήτηρ = mother; υἱός = son; γυνή = woman, wife; πόλις = city, town; νύξ = night)

2.a: 1–d, 2–e, 3–b, 4–f, 5–g, 6–a, 7–h, 8–c (ζητέω = to seek, look for; σῴζω = to save, rescue; ἀκολουθέω = to follow; πορεύομαι = to go, journey; δύναμαι = to be able, can; χαίρω = to rejoice, be glad; βλέπω = to see; ἀποκτείνω = to kill)

3.a: 1–e, 2–d, 3–f, 4–h, 5–g, 6–b, 7–a, 8–c (bonus = good; tōtus = whole, all; similis = like, similar; alius = other, another; tempus = time; quīdam = a certain (one), someone; etiam = also, even; nam = for)

4.a: 1–f, 2–h, 3–b, 4–a, 5–g, 6–c, 7–d, 8–e (θεός = deus; πίστις = fidēs; ζωή = vīta; χαρά = gaudium; ἀλλά = sed; ἐάν = sī; δοῦλος = servus; πνεῦμα = spīritus)

5.why: ἤ normally means “or”; after a comparison it means “than”. Latin: quam.

6.why: ὅμοιος (like) takes the dative. Latin similis takes the dative here too: simile est fermentō.

7.why: αὐτός alone = he; αὐτός next to a noun without article = -self; ὁ αὐτός = the same. Latin: in regiōne eādem, from īdem.

8.a: πορεύομαι, “to go, journey”: aorist passive indicative, 3rd person singular (passive form, active meaning)
8.why: -θη: aorist passive ending, 3rd singular, with the augment ἐ-. πορεύομαι is deponent, so the meaning is active: “he went”.

9.a: ἀποκτείνω, “to kill”: aorist active indicative, 3rd person plural
9.why: A liquid aorist (stem κτειν-, no σ): ἀπέκτεινα, -ας, -εν, … -αν. The augment ε stands after the prefix ἀπο-.

10.a: πίπτω, “to fall”: aorist active indicative, 3rd person singular
10.why: ἔπεσον is the second aorist of πίπτω.

11.a: ἀπόλλυμι, “to destroy; middle: to perish”: future middle indicative, 2nd person plural
11.why: A contracted future (ἀπολέ-εσθε → ἀπολεῖσθε). In the middle voice ἀπόλλυμι means “perish”: “you will perish”.

12.a: πληρόω, “to fill, fulfil”: present passive participle, nominative singular neuter
12.why: -ούμενον: present middle/passive participle of a contract verb (πληρο- + ομενον). Neuter, to agree with τὸ παιδίον: “being filled”.

13.a: ζητέω, “to seek, look for”: aorist active infinitive
13.why: -σαι is the aorist active infinitive ending; the stem vowel ε lengthens to η: ζητη-σαι.

14.a: γίνομαι, “to become, happen”: aorist middle optative, 3rd person singular
14.why: The οι between stem and ending marks the optative, the mood of wishes: “may it happen”.

15.why: -ος is the genitive singular of the third declension (νύξ, νυκτός): “of the night”.

16.a: ἀποδίδωμι, “to give back, pay”: aorist active subjunctive, 2nd person singular
16.why: The ῳ marks the subjunctive of the -μι verb (ἀπο)δίδωμι. After ἕως (until) the subjunctive looks ahead: “until you pay”.

17.a: sequor, sequī, secūtus sum, “to follow”: perfect indicative, 3rd person plural (deponent: passive form, active meaning)
17.why: Deponents form their perfect like a passive: participle + sum. The meaning is active: “they followed”.

18.a: pereō, perīre, periī, peritum, “to perish”: future active indicative, 2nd person plural
18.why: pereō is a compound of eō (go); like eō (ībō, ībis …) it forms its future with -b-: perībō, perībis … perībitis.

19.a: Latin has no active past participle (only deponent verbs such as secūtus, “having followed”, have one). For “having done” it can only use the present participle (faciēns) or a clause.

20.a: It is a Latin idiom: a man “leads” (dūcō) a wife home when he marries. Latin also uses a separate word for wife, uxor, where Greek γυνή means both woman and wife.

21.a: ἀκολουθέω (follow) takes the dative in Greek; Latin sequor takes the accusative. Sequor is also deponent, so secūtī sunt looks passive but means “they followed”.

22.a: Latin has no optative mood. Its subjunctive covers wishes: fīat, “may it happen, let it be”.

23.a: Greek verbs of filling take a genitive of the contents. Latin puts the contents in the ablative (“filled with”), the case Greek lacks.

24.a: Greek: “And he said, ‘A certain man had two sons.’” Latin: “And he said: ‘A certain man had two sons.’”
24.why: τις after a noun means “a certain”: ἄνθρωπός τις = homō quīdam. Greek has the imperfect εἶχεν (was having), Latin the perfect habuit.

25.a: Greek and Latin: “And look, there are last ones who will be first, and there are first ones who will be last.”
25.why: εἰσίν / sunt = there are; ἔσονται / erunt = they will be. The plural adjectives ἔσχατοι / novissimī and πρῶτοι / prīmī are used as nouns: “last ones”, “first ones”.

26.a: Greek: “And he said to them, ‘Then give back the things of Caesar to Caesar, and the things of God to God.’” Latin: “And he said to them: ‘Give back, then, the things that are Caesar’s to Caesar, and the things that are God’s to God.’”
26.why: Greek τά + genitive means “the things of”; Latin has no article, so it needs a clause, quae sunt Caesaris, “the things which are Caesar’s”. The datives Καίσαρι / Caesarī and τῷ θεῷ / Deō mean “to”.

1.a: 1–h, 2–a, 3–g, 4–f, 5–c, 6–b, 7–d, 8–e (κόσμος = world; λόγος = word, message; ἁμαρτία = sin; εἰρήνη = peace; δόξα = glory, honor; ὁδός = way, road; ὕδωρ = water; ἐντολή = command, commandment)

2.a: 1–b, 2–g, 3–e, 4–c, 5–a, 6–h, 7–d, 8–f (θέλω = to want, wish; εὑρίσκω = to find; ἀγαπάω = to love; κρίνω = to judge; τηρέω = to keep, guard; γράφω = to write; ἐσθίω = to eat; περιπατέω = to walk, walk about)

3.a: 1–f, 2–c, 3–d, 4–b, 5–a, 6–g, 7–h, 8–e (mundus = world; via = way, road; aqua = water; pāx = peace; peccātum = sin; glōria = glory; mandātum = command, commandment; sermō = word, speech)

4.a: 1–f, 2–h, 3–g, 4–e, 5–d, 6–c, 7–a, 8–b (ἀγαπάω = dīligō; θέλω = volō; εὑρίσκω = inveniō; γράφω = scrībō; τηρέω = servō; νῦν = nunc; ἤδη = jam; ποῦ = ubi)

5.a: (b) it marks the result as unreal: “you would have”
5.why: ἄν has no English word of its own. With a past indicative it marks a condition contrary to fact. Latin leaves it out and uses the subjunctive (habērētis).

6.why: ἀλλήλων has no nominative, since “one another” is never a subject. Latin uses the adverb invicem.

7.why: οὗτος = this (Latin hic); ἐκεῖνος = that (Latin ille), as in John 1:8, οὐκ ἦν ἐκεῖνος τὸ φῶς / Nōn erat ille lūx.

8.a: θέλω, “to want, wish”: aorist active indicative, 3rd person singular
8.why: The augment of θέλω is ἠ- (ἤθελον, ἠθέλησα); -σεν is the 3rd singular aorist ending.

9.a: λύω, “to loose, destroy”: aorist active imperative, 2nd person plural
9.why: -σατε = aorist σα + -τε, as in ἀκούσατε (Matthew 13:18). λύω, “loose, undo”, here means “tear down!”. Latin solvite.

10.a: ἐγείρω, “to raise, wake”: future active indicative, 1st person singular
10.why: A liquid future: no σ, and a circumflex on the ending (ἐγερῶ, ἐγερεῖς, ἐγερεῖ). Latin excitābō.

11.a: προσκυνέω, “to worship, bow down”: future active indicative, 2nd person plural
11.why: -σετε: future σ plus the 2nd plural ending -ετε. The contract vowel ε lengthens to η before σ.

12.why: φαγ- is the second-aorist stem of ἐσθίω (ἔφαγον), another verb with two stems. -εῖν is the second-aorist infinitive ending.

13.a: ἀγαπάω, “to love”: present active subjunctive, 2nd person plural (after ἵνα; the indicative would look the same)
13.why: In -άω verbs the subjunctive (ἀγαπα-ητε) and the indicative (ἀγαπα-ετε) both contract to ἀγαπᾶτε; ἵνα, which takes the subjunctive, tells you which it is. Latin dīligātis is subjunctive too.

14.a: ἀγαπάω, “to love”: aorist active indicative, 1st person singular
14.why: Augment ἠ-, stem vowel α lengthened to η before σ, and the ending -σα: “I loved”. Latin dīlēxī.

15.a: γράφω, “to write”: perfect active indicative, 1st person singular
15.why: Reduplication γε- and the ending -α mark the perfect: the writing is done and stands. Latin scrīpsī.

16.why: -αις is the dative plural of the first declension. ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις = “in three days” (time within which).

17.a: videō, vidēre, vīdī, vīsum, “to see”: future active indicative, 3rd person singular
17.why: 2nd-conjugation futures use -b-: vidēbō, vidēbis, vidēbit. Here it renders the strong Greek negation οὐ μὴ θεωρήσῃ.

18.a: “This” refers to the Word. In Greek, λόγος is masculine, so οὗτος; in Latin, verbum is neuter, so hoc. Each pronoun agrees with its own language’s noun.

19.a: ἀκολουθέω takes the dative; Latin sequor takes the accusative. (Sequere is the imperative of the deponent sequor, passive in form but active in meaning.)

20.a: In Greek a neuter plural subject usually takes a singular verb (ἔστιν). Latin has no such rule, so the plural subject verba takes a plural verb (sunt).

21.a: οὐ μή + aorist subjunctive is the strongest Greek denial of a future event: “he will never see”. Latin has no such idiom and uses a plain negative future, nōn vidēbit.

22.a: Greek uses past tenses of the indicative (ἦτε, εἴχετε) plus ἄν in the result. Latin uses the imperfect subjunctive in both halves (essētis, habērētis).
22.why: Both mean: “If you were blind (but you are not), you would not have sin.”

23.a: Greek: “He was in the world, and the world came to be through him, and the world did not know him.” Latin: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him.”
23.why: The subject “he” is inside the verbs ἦν / erat. Greek δι’ αὐτοῦ = Latin per ipsum, “through him”.

24.a: Greek and Latin: “I and the Father are one.”
24.why: Both languages use the neuter, “one thing”, not the masculine “one person”: ἕν / ūnum. The verb is 1st person plural: ἐσμέν / sumus, “we are”.

25.a: Greek: “If you know these things, you are blessed if you do them.” Latin: “If you know these things, you will be blessed if you do them” (word for word: “if you will have done them”).
25.why: Latin looks forward: future eritis (“you will be”) and future perfect fēceritis, where Greek has the present ἐστε and ἐάν + present subjunctive. αὐτά and ea are both neuter plural: “them (these things)”.

1.a: 1–f, 2–c, 3–d, 4–g, 5–a, 6–e, 7–h, 8–b (ἅγιος = holy; plural as a noun: saints; κατοικέω = to dwell, live; σπέρμα = seed, offspring; ἐπαγγελία = promise; πρόσωπον = face; λαός = people; βαπτίζω = to baptize, immerse; γλῶσσα = tongue, language)

2.a: 1–f, 2–d, 3–a, 4–b, 5–c, 6–g, 7–h, 8–e (ἅγιος = sānctus; κατοικέω = habitō; σπέρμα = sēmen; πρόσωπον = faciēs; λαός = populus; βαπτίζω = baptīzō; λαλέω = loquor; γλῶσσα = lingua)

3.a: (b) never first: after the first word of what it joins
3.why: Like δέ and γάρ, τε is never placed first. Latin puts et in front: et loquēbantur.

4.why: πρό takes the genitive. “Before the face of” is a Hebrew way of saying “ahead of”. Latin: ante faciem.

5.a: (b) passive in form but active in meaning
5.why: loquēbantur looks passive but means “they were speaking”. Greek deponents such as ἔρχομαι work the same way.

6.a: διέρχομαι, “to go through”: present middle participle, accusative singular masculine (deponent: middle form, active meaning)

7.a: κατοικέω, “to dwell, live”: present active participle, accusative plural masculine
7.why: Contract verb: κατοικε- + οντας → κατοικοῦντας. With τοὺς: “those living (in Lydda)”.

8.a: ἄγω, “to lead, bring”: aorist active indicative, 3rd person singular
8.why: ἤγαγον is the reduplicated second aorist of ἄγω (ἀγ- doubled to ἀγαγ-, then augmented).

9.a: βαπτίζω, “to baptize, immerse”: aorist passive indicative, 3rd person plural
9.why: -θησαν: the aorist passive sign θη plus the 3rd plural ending -σαν: “they were baptized”.

10.a: ἐπιτίθημι, “to lay on, put on”: aorist active participle, genitive singular masculine
10.why: From ἐπι + τίθημι. -θέντος is the genitive of the aorist active participle (θείς, θέντος). With τοῦ Παύλου it forms a genitive absolute: “Paul having laid on (hands)”.

11.a: λαλέω, “to speak, talk”: imperfect active indicative, 3rd person plural (the same form can also be 1st person singular)
11.why: Augment ἐ- plus the contraction λαλε- + ον: ἐ-λαλε-ον → ἐλάλουν, the imperfect, an action going on: “they were speaking”.

12.a: γλῶσσα, “tongue, language”: noun, dative plural feminine
12.why: -αις: first-declension dative plural, “in/with tongues”. Latin linguīs (ablative).

13.a: σπέρμα, “seed, offspring”: noun, genitive singular neuter
13.why: -ματος: genitive singular of a neuter noun in -μα (σπέρμα, σπέρματος), after ἀπό.

14.a: baptīzō, baptīzāre, baptīzāvī, baptīzātum, “to baptize”: perfect passive indicative, 3rd person plural
14.why: The perfect passive is the perfect participle (baptīzātī, masculine plural) + sunt. It renders the Greek aorist passive ἐβαπτίσθησαν.

15.a: loquor, loquī, locūtus sum, “to speak”: imperfect indicative, 3rd person plural (deponent: passive form, active meaning)
15.why: -bā- marks the imperfect; -ntur is a passive ending, but loquor is deponent: “they were speaking”, like Greek ἐλάλουν.

16.a: Latin turns the infinitive into an ut-clause with a subjunctive (dēvenīret), “it happened that Peter came down”. In a clause the subject is nominative.

17.a: Greek uses a genitive absolute and Latin an ablative absolute: a noun and participle set apart from the main sentence, “John having proclaimed beforehand”.
17.why: praedicante. — Outside deponent verbs Latin has no active past participle, so it uses the present participle

18.a: Latin has no active past participle (except in deponent verbs). It uses the perfect passive participle in an ablative absolute: hīs audītīs.

19.a: Latin uses in with the ablative (“in the name”), not in with the accusative (“into”). The Greek idiom of motion “into” the name becomes “in” the name.

20.a: Greek: “And for three days he was without sight, and he did not eat or drink.” (word for word: “he was three days not seeing, and did not eat nor drink”). Latin: “And he was there for three days, not seeing, and he did not eat, nor drink.”
20.why: Greek puts the length of time in the accusative (ἡμέρας τρεῖς); Latin here uses the ablative (tribus diēbus) and adds ibi, “there”. With a participle the negative is μή: μὴ βλέπων / nōn vidēns.

21.a: Greek and Latin: “For we cannot stop speaking about the things we have seen and heard.” (word for word: “For we are not able not to speak the things which we saw and heard.”)
21.why: Two negatives make a strong positive: “we cannot not speak”. γάρ and enim (for) never stand first in their sentence.

22.a: Greek and Latin: “And I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And the Lord said, ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.’”
22.why: κύριε / domine are vocatives (direct address); ὁ κύριος / Dominus are nominative subjects. ὅν / quem (whom) are accusative, the object of the verb.

1.a: 1–e, 2–c, 3–h, 4–f, 5–g, 6–b, 7–a, 8–d (ἀδελφός = brother; νόμος = law; ἐκκλησία = assembly, church; σάρξ = flesh; ἔργον = work, deed; ἐλπίς = hope; ἀγάπη = love; ἀλήθεια = truth)

2.a: 1–f, 2–h, 3–e, 4–b, 5–c, 6–a, 7–d, 8–g (ζάω = to live; καλέω = to call; ἁμαρτάνω = to sin; φοβέομαι = to fear, be afraid; πάσχω = to suffer; βάλλω = to throw, cast; αἰτέω = to ask, request; γεννάω = to father; to give birth to)

3.a: 1–h, 2–f, 3–g, 4–e, 5–c, 6–d, 7–a, 8–b (semper = always; sine = without; sīc = thus, in this way; itaque = and so, therefore; propter = because of, on account of; post = after; cōram = in the presence of, before; nisi = unless, except)

4.a: 1–c, 2–d, 3–h, 4–f, 5–a, 6–b, 7–e, 8–g (ἀδελφός = frāter; νόμος = lēx; ἐλπίς = spēs; ἀγάπη = cāritās; ἀλήθεια = vēritās; φόβος = timor; πῦρ = ignis; σάρξ = carō)

5.why: σύν always takes the dative. Compare μετά, which means “with” when it takes the genitive (μετ’ ἐμοῦ). Latin joins cum to the pronoun: mēcum.

6.why: Latin: prō vōbīs. (With the accusative ὑπέρ means “above, beyond”.)

7.why: καί + ἐγώ = κἀγώ, “I too, and I”. Latin keeps the words apart: et ego.

8.a: ζάω, “to live”: present active indicative, 3rd person singular
8.why: ζάω contracts with η, not α: ζῶ, ζῇς, ζῇ. So ζῇ is “he lives”. (The Latin is vīvit.)

9.a: ἀσπάζομαι, “to greet, salute”: aorist middle imperative, 2nd person plural (deponent: middle form, active meaning)
9.why: -σασθε: aorist σα + the middle ending -σθε. A plural command: “greet!”

10.a: φοβέομαι, “to fear, be afraid”: present middle indicative, 1st person singular (middle/passive form, active meaning)
10.why: Contract verb: φοβε- + ομαι → φοβοῦμαι, “I am afraid”.

11.a: διδάσκω, “to teach”: aorist passive indicative, 2nd person plural
11.why: The aorist passive sign θη (διδαχ-θη-) plus the 2nd plural ending -τε: “you were taught”. Latin turns it round: didicistis, “you learned”.

12.a: ἀγαπάω, “to love”: present active participle, nominative singular masculine
12.why: Contract verb: ἀγαπα- + ων → ἀγαπῶν. With ὁ μή: “the one who does not love”.

13.a: γινώσκω, “to know”: aorist active indicative, 3rd person singular
13.why: A root aorist of γινώσκω: ἔγνων, ἔγνως, ἔγνω. Latin translates with the perfect nōvit, “has come to know, knows”.

14.a: γεννάω, “to father; passive: to be born”: perfect passive indicative, 3rd person singular
14.why: Reduplication γε- and the ending -ται with no thematic vowel: perfect middle/passive, “he has been born”.

15.why: A third-declension noun with stem ἐλπιδ-: ἐλπίς, ἐλπίδος; -α is the accusative singular ending.

16.a: ἀνήρ, “man, husband”: noun, accusative plural masculine
16.why: ἀνήρ, ἀνδρός: third declension; -ας is the accusative plural. Here the subject of the infinitive προσεύχεσθαι.

17.a: dīligō, dīligere, dīlēxī, dīlēctum, “to love”: perfect active indicative, 3rd person singular
17.why: The perfect stem dīlēx- plus -it. It renders the Greek aorist ἠγάπησεν.

18.a: nāscor, nāscī, nātus sum, “to be born”: perfect indicative, 3rd person singular (deponent: passive form, active meaning)
18.why: Perfect participle nātus + est: “he has been born”, matching the Greek perfect passive γεγέννηται.

19.a: For “my” Latin uses the possessive adjective meus, which agrees with the noun it describes: meam, accusative singular feminine like mātrem. Greek often uses the genitive of the pronoun instead.

20.a: πείθω (persuade) takes an accusative object. Latin suādeō means “advise, urge” and takes a dative of the person: “do I urge (it) on people?”.

21.a: With nōlī (plural nōlīte), the imperative of nōlō, “be unwilling”, plus an infinitive: “do not receive”.

22.a: A genitive absolute in Greek and an ablative absolute in Latin: “when we sin by choice”, a participle phrase set apart from the main clause.

23.a: After a verb of fearing both mean “that” (“I am afraid that I have toiled in vain”). Latin follows nē with a subjunctive (labōrāverim).

24.a: Greek: “But now faith, hope, love remain, these three; and the greatest of these is love.” (word for word: “and greater of these is the love”). Latin: “But now faith, hope, love remain, these three; and the greatest of these is love.”
24.why: Greek has a singular verb (μένει) with three subjects, Latin a plural (manent). Greek needs no “is” in the last clause; Latin adds est. The comparative “greater” is used for the greatest of three.

25.a: Greek and Latin: “So then the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.”
25.why: Neither language uses a verb (“is”). Greek ἁγία, δικαία, ἀγαθή are feminine to agree with ἐντολή; Latin sānctum, jūstum, bonum are neuter to agree with mandātum, and sāncta is feminine for lēx.

26.a: Greek and Latin: “They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.”
26.why: ἀκούω takes a genitive of the person heard (αὐτῶν); Latin audiō takes an accusative (eōs). Greek ἐκ / Latin dē: “from, out of”.

1.a: 1–b, 2–a, 3–e, 4–g, 5–f, 6–d, 7–h, 8–c (θηρίον = wild animal, beast; νεκρός = dead; ἄχρι = until, as far as; ἔτος = year; σοφία = wisdom; λοιπός = remaining; οἱ λοιποί = the rest; πρῶτος = first; ἀνάστασις = resurrection, rising)

2.a: 1–d, 2–a, 3–g, 4–e, 5–b, 6–c, 7–h, 8–f (bestia = beast; mīlle = a thousand; annus = year; sapientia = wisdom; cēterus = the other, the rest; prīmus = first; mortuus = dead; vīvō = to live)

3.a: 1–f, 2–e, 3–b, 4–a, 5–d, 6–c (εἷς = ūnus; δύο = duo; τρεῖς = trēs; ἑπτά = septem; δώδεκα = duodecim; χίλιοι = mīlle)

4.why: ἑξακόσιοι = six hundred, ἑξήκοντα = sixty, ἕξ = six. Latin: sexcentī sexāgintā sex.

5.why: ἕξ and sex (six), like ἑπτά and septem (seven), go back to the same ancestor word.

6.a: ψηφίζω, “to count, calculate”: aorist active imperative, 3rd person singular
6.why: -σάτω is the 3rd singular aorist imperative ending: “let him count”. Greek has 3rd-person commands; English needs “let”.

7.a: ἔχω, “to have, hold”: present active participle, nominative singular masculine
7.why: With ὁ: “the one having”, that is, whoever has (insight).

8.a: ζάω, “to live”: aorist active indicative, 3rd person plural
8.why: Augment ἐ- + ζη-σαν: “they came to life”. The aorist marks the start of living.

9.a: τελέω, “to finish, complete”: aorist passive subjunctive, 3rd person singular
9.why: -θῇ: aorist passive subjunctive, used after ἄχρι (until). It is singular although τὰ χίλια ἔτη is plural, because the subject is neuter plural.

10.why: ἔτος, ἔτους is a neuter noun of the third declension; -η is the nominative/accusative plural (from ἔτεα).

11.why: -ῶν is genitive plural. With τῶν, an adjective used as a noun: “of the dead”.

12.a: θηρίον, “wild animal, beast”: noun, genitive singular neuter
12.why: -ου is the genitive singular of a second-declension neuter noun in -ον.

13.a: computō, computāre, computāvī, computātum, “to count, calculate”: present active subjunctive, 3rd person singular
13.why: In a 1st-conjugation verb the vowel e (computet, not computat) marks the subjunctive. Here it gives a command: “let him count”.

14.a: vīvō, vīvere, vīxī, vīctum, “to live”: perfect active indicative, 3rd person plural
14.why: The perfect stem vīx- (vīvō, vīxī) plus -ērunt. It renders the Greek aorist ἔζησαν.

15.a: Latin normally gives a 3rd-person command with the present subjunctive (a “jussive” subjunctive): computet, “let him count”.

16.a: In Greek a neuter plural subject (τὰ ἔτη) takes a singular verb. Latin annī is masculine plural and takes a plural verb.

17.a: Latin adds est (“is”), which Greek can leave unspoken. It leaves out the two articles (ἡ … ἡ), since Latin has no article.

18.a: Latin has no article to turn a participle into a noun, so it uses a relative clause: quī habet, “who has”.

19.a: Greek: “So write the things you saw, and the things that are, and the things that are about to happen after these things.” Latin: “Write therefore the things you saw, and the things that are, and the things that must happen after these things.”
19.why: Where Greek has μέλλει γίνεσθαι, “is about to happen”, Latin says oportet fierī, “must happen”. μετὰ ταῦτα / post haec = after these things.

20.a: Greek: “And the woman whom you saw is the great city that has rule over the kings of the earth” (word for word: “the city, the great one, the one having a kingdom over the kings of the earth”). Latin: “And the woman whom you saw is the great city which has rule over the kings of the earth.”
20.why: Greek repeats the article (ἡ πόλις ἡ μεγάλη ἡ ἔχουσα); Latin has none and uses a relative clause, quae habet, for the participle.

21.a: Greek and Latin: “And they will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.”
21.why: The second half has no verb in either language; English supplies “will be”. αὐτοῦ / ejus = his; αὐτῶν / eōrum = their.

1.a: 1–d, 2–h, 3–f, 4–b, 5–j, 6–g, 7–i, 8–a, 9–c, 10–e (βασιλεία = kingdom; ἔρχομαι = to come, go; γινώσκω = to know; ὄχλος = crowd; καρδία = heart; ζητέω = to seek; κόσμος = world; ἀγαπάω = to love; λαός = people; ἐλπίς = hope)

2.a: 1–b, 2–a, 3–d, 4–e, 5–i, 6–h, 7–f, 8–c, 9–j, 10–g (autem = however (never first in its clause); enim = for; ergō = therefore, so; quia = because; sī = if; nunc = now; jam = already; semper = always; statim = at once; iterum = again)

3.a: 1–h, 2–c, 3–d, 4–a, 5–b, 6–g, 7–f, 8–e (λέγω = dīcō; ὁράω = videō; ποιέω = faciō; δίδωμι = dō; ἔχω = habeō; ἀκούω = audiō; πιστεύω = crēdō; γράφω = scrībō)

4.a: 1–b, 2–e, 3–d, 4–f, 5–c, 6–a (εἶπον = λέγω; ἦλθον = ἔρχομαι; εἶδον = ὁράω; ἔφαγον = ἐσθίω; ἤνεγκα = φέρω; ἔλαβον = λαμβάνω)

6.why: ἐν τῇ ἐσχάτῃ ἡμέρᾳ / in novissimō diē, “on the last day” (John 11:24).

7.why: -ους accusative plural, -ων genitive plural, -οι nominative plural.

8.a: (a) τοῦ: genitive singular, masculine or neuter. (b) τά: nominative or accusative plural, neuter.

9.a: (a) a past tense of the indicative
9.why: The augment appears only in the indicative of the past tenses: imperfect, aorist, pluperfect.

10.why: The optative is rare in the New Testament and mostly expresses wishes. Latin uses the subjunctive: fīat.

11.why: For example προκηρύξαντος Ἰωάννου / praedicante Jōanne (Acts 13:24); Latin may also use a cum-clause.

12.a: (b) middle or passive in form but active in meaning

13.why: Greek says μετ’ ἐμοῦ, μεθ’ ὑμῶν, μετ’ αὐτοῦ (Matthew 12:30, John 13:33, Mark 14:33).

14.why: “Surely no one brought him anything to eat?” Latin uses numquid, which also expects “no”.

15.why: hīc (long ī) is the adverb “here” (Greek ὧδε); hic (short i) is “this” (Greek οὗτος).

16.a: (b) dative, because ἐν takes the dative
16.why: ἐν always takes the dative. τῆς θαλάσσης is genitive, “of the sea”.

17.a: ἐκ + genitive; Latin ex (or ē) + ablative. Before a vowel ἐκ becomes ἐξ: ἐξ αὐτοῦ (Mark 5:30, 14:23).
17.why: Latin often uses dē + ablative for the same idea: dē illō (Mark 5:30).

18.a: γίνομαι, “to become, happen”: aorist middle participle, genitive singular feminine
18.why: Second-aorist middle participle (γεν- + ομένης), genitive singular feminine to agree with ὀψίας: a genitive absolute, “evening having come”.

19.a: ἵστημι, “to stand; to set”: aorist active indicative, 3rd person plural (here “they stood still”)
19.why: In this form both aorists of ἵστημι look the same; here the sense is intransitive: “they stood still”.

20.a: τίθημι, “to put, place”: present active indicative, 3rd person singular
20.why: A -μι verb: reduplicated stem τι-θη- and the ending -σι(ν). Compare δίδωσιν, “he gives” (John 14:27).

21.a: αἴρω, “to lift, take away”: aorist active imperative, 2nd person singular
21.why: A liquid aorist (ἦρα, from αἴρω); -ον is the 2nd singular aorist imperative ending: “lift up!”. Latin tolle.

22.a: ἀνίστημι, “to raise; to rise”: future middle indicative, 3rd person singular
22.why: ἀνά + ἵστημι; future σ + middle ending -εται. In the middle it means “rise”: “he will rise”.

23.a: καλέω, “to call”: present passive participle, nominative singular masculine
23.why: Contract verb: καλε- + όμενος → καλούμενος, “being called”. Latin uses a clause: quī vocātur.

24.a: ἐγείρω, “to raise, wake”: present passive imperative, 2nd person plural (“get up!”)
24.why: -εσθε is the present middle/passive 2nd plural (here an imperative): “be raised, get up!”. Latin surgite.

25.a: τηρέω, “to keep, guard”: aorist active subjunctive, 3rd person singular
25.why: The long vowel η and the iota subscript (-σῃ) mark the aorist subjunctive, as required after ἐάν: “if someone keeps”.

26.a: videō, vidēre, vīdī, vīsum, “to see”: perfect active indicative, 3rd person plural
26.why: The perfect stem vīd- has a long ī. It renders the Greek aorist εἶδον, “they saw”.

27.a: dīcō, dīcere, dīxī, dictum, “to say”: imperfect active indicative, 3rd person singular
27.why: -ēba- marks the imperfect of a 3rd-conjugation verb: “he was saying”, matching Greek ἔλεγεν.

28.a: crēdō, crēdere, crēdidī, crēditum, “to believe”: present active subjunctive, 2nd person plural
28.why: In the 3rd conjugation the subjunctive has -a-: crēdam, crēdās, crēdat … crēdātis. After ut (so that) the verb is subjunctive, as after Greek ἵνα (πιστεύσητε).

29.a: A genitive absolute in Greek and an ablative absolute in Latin: a noun with a participle, set apart from the main clause: “with the feast already half over”.

30.a: Greek verbs of filling take a genitive of the contents. Latin uses its ablative (“with water”), a case Greek does not have.

31.a: Latin expresses “our” with the possessive adjective noster, which agrees with oculīs (ablative plural). Greek uses the genitive of the pronoun.

32.a: Greek uses ἄν with a past tense of the indicative (ἤμην). Latin uses the imperfect subjunctive (essem) and has no word for ἄν.

33.a: Latin sum (be) has no present participle, so there is no Latin word for “being”. Latin uses a relative clause: quī erant.

34.why: Latin has no aorist. Its perfect does the work of both the Greek aorist (“they came”) and the Greek perfect (“they have come”).

35.a: “God is love.” ἀγάπη has no article because it is the predicate; the subject ὁ θεός has the article.
35.why: Latin has no article in either word; word order and sense tell you that Deus is the subject.

36.a: “What I have written, I have written.” γέγραφα is a perfect: the writing is done and stands.
36.why: Latin scrīpsī is a perfect too; it can mean “I wrote” or “I have written”.

37.a: Greek: “The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand” (word for word: “in his hand”). Latin: “The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand.”
37.why: ἀγαπᾷ / dīligit: present, “loves”. τὸν υἱόν / Fīlium: accusative object. The Greek perfect δέδωκεν becomes the Latin perfect dedit.

38.a: Greek and Latin: “But he, passing through the middle of them, went on his way.”
38.why: αὐτὸς / ipse: “he himself”. διὰ μέσου αὐτῶν / per medium illōrum: “through the middle of them”.

39.a: Greek: “one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all” (word for word: “the one over all”). Latin: “one God and Father of all, who is over all, and through all things, and in us all.”
39.why: Greek ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων, article + phrase, “the one over all”, needs no verb; Latin turns it into a clause, quī est super omnēs, and adds nōbīs, “in us all”.

40.a: Greek: “And he appointed twelve, so that they might be with him and so that he might send them out to preach.” Latin: “And he brought it about that twelve should be with him, and that he might send them to preach.”
40.why: Both languages use a subjunctive after “so that”: ἵνα ὦσιν / ut essent; ἵνα ἀποστέλλῃ / ut mitteret. Latin fēcit ut … means “he brought it about that …”.
